title: Visual Implicit Autoregressive Modeling
relevance_reason: Replaces VAR's explicit middle stack with one weight-tied implicit (DEQ) layer between 5 pre and 5 post blocks, with a per-scale iteration knob at inference.
one_sentence: Next-scale visual AR generator whose middle stack is a single implicit equilibrium layer trained with stochastic Jacobian-free backprop; at 770.9M parameters it nearly matches the 2.0B VAR-d30 on ImageNet-256 FID with less memory and fewer FLOPs.
key_contributions: Sandwich design: p=5 explicit pre-blocks, one implicit fixed-point layer with input-injection projection, p=5 post-blocks; S-JFB with random N in 0-10 no-grad and M in 1-12 with-grad iterations.
Per-scale iteration schedules (constant, decreasing, residual-threshold) as an inference-time compute knob; iteration-indexed KV cache.
Fixed-point iterations converge in about 10 steps; reallocating iterations from fine to coarse scales gives better quality-efficiency trade-offs.

title: Self-composing neural operators for high-frequency and multiscale PDE surrogates
relevance_reason: Deep neural operator built by repeatedly applying one tied backbone block, trained with a depth-growing Train-and-Unroll curriculum; with approximation theory in the composition depth.
one_sentence: Neural operator P o G^n o L with one shared backbone block G (multigrid-style MgNO), trained by progressively growing n; matches untied operators on Darcy with fewer parameters and cuts Helmholtz/USCT error versus FNO-type baselines.
key_contributions: Self-composing operator: lifting, n compositions of a single tied backbone, projection; universal approximation (Thm 1) and error decay with depth n (Thm 2).
Train-and-Unroll: train depth l, warm-start depth l+1 from the converged shallower model, yielding a family of usable intermediate-depth models.
Controlled regular-vs-self ablation: self-composition helps the multigrid backbone but not FNO or UNet.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: USCT: 7,200 training pairs, 900 test; ablation on 25% subset (1,790 train); Darcy benchmarks
setup.baselines: untied FNO2D, MgNO, UNet, AFNO, BFNO, Galerkin Transformer, LSM
setup.benchmarks: Darcy smooth/rough, multiscale Darcy, USCT Helmholtz 300/400/500 kHz, OT Car-CFD

claims.evidence_quote: It is worth noting, however, that lower parameter count does not by itself imply lower activation memory or shorter wall-clock training time.

claims.claim: In a controlled 400 kHz ablation, self-composition helps only the multigrid backbone; regular FNO and UNet are slightly better than their self-composed versions.
claims.evidence_quote: For FNO and UNet, the regular and self-composed variants remain close, with the regular models slightly better in this short run (0.0902 versus 0.0966 for FNO and 0.2559 versus 0.2610 for UNet).

claims.claim: Train-and-Unroll reaches lower loss than direct training at the target depth; training error decays nearly geometrically with depth then saturates above machine precision.
claims.evidence_quote: T&U reaches lower loss than direct target-depth training while still providing usable intermediate models O(3) and O(4) before the final O(5)

numbers.what: USCT validation RRMSE at 400 kHz, MgNO regular vs self
numbers.quote: The clearest gain appears in the multigridinspired backbone, where MgNO-self reaches 0.0151 compared with 0.0194

numbers.what: USCT RRMSE reduction vs spectral baselines
numbers.quote: with about 9–13× RRMSE reductions relative to the spectral baselines.

numbers.what: USCT training setup
numbers.quote: The training set consists of 7,200 multiscale sound speed map and wave field pairs, and evaluation is performed on a held-out 900-sample test set at 300, 400, and 500 kHz.

numbers.quote: the staged T&U schedule reduces total training time from 32.04 h for direct target-depth training to 23.96 h, a measured 25.2% saving.

numbers.what: final validation loss over 3 seeds, direct vs T&U
numbers.quote: Across three separate random initialization seeds under the same setup, direct training finishes with final validation loss 0.0194 ± 0.0015, whereas T&U reaches 0.0151 ± 0.0012.

limitations: Depth growth saturates at a nonzero error floor; no FLOP or hardware-normalized comparison; controlled self-vs-regular ablation only on a 25% subset and short runs; tying does not save activation memory.
survey_notes: Beyond-language (science/PDE). Explicitly contrasts with DEQs (explicit depth, no fixed-point solve) and with unrolling (tied, not stage-specific). Train-and-Unroll is a depth curriculum analogous to progressive-loop curricula in LMs. Mixed evidence: tying helps the multigrid backbone (whose block mimics a solver step) but not FNO/UNet, supporting the view that recurrence helps when the block matches an iterative algorithm. Activation memory not saved, consistent with LM looped findings. Confound: the MgNO regular-vs-self numbers in Table 3 (0.0194 vs 0.0151) are identical to the direct-training-vs-T&U numbers in Sec. 3, and self-composed models are trained with T&U while regular baselines are trained directly, so the MgNO self-composition gain is not separated from the curriculum.

title: Learning to Stop Overthinking at Test Time
relevance_reason: Deep-thinking-style recurrent vision model that iterates one recurrent conv layer and picks the halting iteration at test time via a self-supervised proxy task.
one_sentence: Recurrent conv models (Conv-GRU and a simplified Conv-LiGRU) trained on clean CIFAR generalize to corrupted CIFAR-C by iterating longer; a rotation-prediction auxiliary head selects the per-sample stopping iteration, reducing overthinking.
key_contributions: Test-time halting: choose the iteration with peak self-supervised (rotation-prediction) accuracy as a proxy for main-task accuracy, instead of halt-early heuristics such as ACT.
Conv-LiGRU: Conv-GRU with simplified reset gate and ReLU, more stable across iterations than Conv-GRU and less prone to overthinking.
Recurrent models use about one-sixth the parameters of a ResNet and need more iterations for harder corruption levels.

setup.loops_test: variable; selected per sample by auxiliary task
setup.baselines: ResNet (feed-forward), Deep Thinking Recall, Conv-GRU, ACT halting
setup.benchmarks: CIFAR10-C, CIFAR100-C level 5

claims.claim: A recurrent model with 24 iterations outperforms a feed-forward network of equivalent computational depth, and harder corruption levels need more iterations to reach the same accuracy.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (stated; details of the matched network not given)
claims.evidence_quote: Notably, a recurrent model with 24 iterations outperforms a feed-forward network with equivalent computational depth, emphasizing the effectiveness of dynamic depth adjustment.

claims.claim: Recurrent models use about one-sixth the parameters of feed-forward networks while generalizing better to corruptions.
claims.evidence_quote: Recurrent models also demonstrate remarkable parameter efficiency, as shown in Table 1, using only one-sixth the parameters of feed-forward networks while achieving superior generalization.

claims.claim: Halting-as-early-as-possible heuristics (ACT) limit extrapolation; selecting the iteration by self-supervised accuracy performs better.
claims.evidence_quote: We show that the early stopping heuristic in previous works—which forces the model to halt as soon as possible—limits the extrapolation capabilities of RNNs.

numbers.what: iterations needed to reach 60% accuracy at noise level 3 vs 5
numbers.quote: at noise level 3, the model requires just 6 iterations to achieve 60% accuracy, while at noise level 5, it needs 13 iterations to achieve the same accuracy.

numbers.what: average accuracy gain of Conv-LiGRU over Conv-GRU on CIFAR100-C level 5
numbers.quote: With an average accuracy improvement of 0.98% (as shown in Table 3), these findings underscore Conv-LiGRU's remarkable effectiveness

limitations: Rotation prediction is an unreliable proxy for images with few edge features or isotropic content (Sec. 4.6); small CIFAR-scale experiments only.
survey_notes: Adaptive depth / beyond-language: an unsupervised test-time halting signal for recurrent-depth models, an alternative to learned halting (ACT/PonderNet) and convergence criteria. Reports overthinking for Conv-GRU while DT-Recall resists it, consistent with 2202.05826. Iso-depth claim is qualitative (Fig. 3) without stated architecture of the matched feed-forward net.

title: FlexiGPT: Pruning and Extending Large Language Models with Low-Rank Weight Sharing
relevance_reason: Retrofits pretrained LLMs with relaxed weight sharing: pruned blocks are replaced by reused unpruned blocks plus block-specific LoRA, and small models are deepened by repeating blocks with unique LoRA.
one_sentence: Prunes LLM blocks by importance and replaces each with a weight-shared unpruned block plus SVD-initialized LoRA and output normalization; also extends TinyLlama from 22 to 36 effective layers by repeating blocks with unique adapters.
key_contributions: Weight-sharing replacement of pruned blocks chosen by a principled score, with block-specific low-rank adapters initialized from SVD reconstruction and small-initialized output normalization.
Model extension: repeat block ranges (block-wise or sequential patterns) with unique LoRA and normalization, a relaxed-sharing depth retrofit.
Self-speculative decoding that drafts with the pruned model without replacement blocks and verifies with the full model.

title: Merging Feed-Forward Sublayers for Compressed Transformers
relevance_reason: Post-hoc cross-layer tying of FFN sublayers in pretrained Transformers (component-level sharing); depth is unchanged, no looping of compute.
one_sentence: Aligns (by neuron permutation), averages and ties FFN sublayers of k consecutive layers in pretrained GPT-2, ViT and OPUS-MT, then recovery-finetunes; removing a third of FFN sublayers costs about 1% ViT accuracy, 1 PPL, 2 BLEU.
key_contributions: Post-training FFN weight tying via permutation alignment to an anchor layer, then merging and recovery fine-tuning.
Matches or beats a layer-dropping baseline at comparable parameter reduction on three tasks.
Observes high activation similarity among some FFN sublayers separated by attention, suggesting why they are mergeable.

title: Transformer Layers as Painters
relevance_reason: Training-free interventions on frozen LLMs, including replacing middle layers by repeats of the center layer and looping a parallelized middle block; informs training-free looping and retrofitting.
one_sentence: Frozen-model ablations on Llama2 and BERT show first/last layers are distinct while middle layers share a representation space; replacing middle layers with repeats of one layer is catastrophic, but looping the averaged parallel middle block helps.
key_contributions: Middle layers share a representation space (high cosine similarity) but are not redundant: weight-sharing them via repetition of the center layer is the worst intervention.
Layer order matters more for math/reasoning (GSM8K) than for semantic tasks; skipping, reversing, randomizing and parallelizing middle layers degrade gracefully otherwise.
Looped Parallel: feeding the mean output of parallel middle layers back for several iterations beats a single parallel pass; optimal iterations scale roughly with the number of parallelized layers.

claims.evidence_quote: Yes, with the optimal number of iterations proportional to the number of parallelized layers.

claims.evidence_quote: Yes! Mathematical and reasoning tasks are more order dependent than "semantic" tasks.

Suggests trained looped models need training to make a block reusable; untrained repetition of one layer fails.

title: Transformers Learn to Implement Multi-step Gradient Descent with Chain of Thought
relevance_reason: Training-dynamics theory of CoT on in-context weight prediction; includes a theorem improving the looped-transformer optimization result of Gatmiry et al. and a looped vs non-looped separation.
one_sentence: Proves a one-layer linear transformer without CoT can only do one GD step on in-context weight prediction while CoT training provably learns multi-step GD; the same technique shows looped linear transformers with L = Theta(log d) loops beat non-looped ones.
key_contributions: Expressiveness gap: global optimum of one-layer linear attention without CoT equals one GD step; with CoT, Theta(log d) autoregressive steps reach near-exact recovery.
Gradient-flow convergence on the population CoT loss plus in- and out-of-distribution generalization.
Theorem 4.3: improves Gatmiry et al.'s looped-transformer analysis so looped transformers provably beat the one-step non-looped transformer (loss strictly better for L >= 2).

setup.baselines: one-layer transformer without CoT / without looping
setup.benchmarks: evaluation loss on in-context weight prediction

claims.claim: With loops L = Omega(log d), the looped linear transformer's global minimizer reaches arbitrarily small polynomial loss and is strictly better than the non-looped one-layer transformer for L >= 2.

claims.evidence_quote: Moreover, the asymptotic loss is strictly better than that of the non-looped one-layer transformer when L ≥ 2, thus establishing the separation between looped and non-looped transformers.

claims.claim: Gatmiry et al.'s earlier bound for looped transformers implementing multi-step GD was no better than a single GD step; this paper closes that gap.
claims.evidence_quote: Notably, the looped transformer in [20] that implements multi-step gradient descent is shown to be no better than the transformer performing a single gradient descent step.

claims.claim: CoT and looping are two routes to the same iterative algorithm: both can naturally implement gradient descent.
claims.evidence_quote: The key connection between our work and Gatmiry et al. [20] lies in the observation that both looped transformers and transformers with CoT prompting through autoregressive generation are capable of naturally implementing iterative algorithms like gradient descent.

title: TroL: Traversal of Layers for Large Language and Vision Models
relevance_reason: Each LLM layer is applied twice (L(L(x))) and mixed token-wise with L(x) by a learned gate, i.e., per-layer looping retrofitted into pretrained multimodal LLMs.
one_sentence: Vision-language models (1.8B/3.8B/7B) where every layer is re-applied once and a tiny token-wise gate mixes L(x) and L(L(x)); with 49K-131K extra parameters it gains about 10 points on MMStar/MM-Vet over the same model without traversal.
key_contributions: Layer traversing: per-layer double application with TroL-Mixer, (1-w)*L(x) + w*L(L(x)), with w from a token-wise TroL Gating module.
Two-step training (projector + mixers, then QLoRA on the backbone) on 2.3M visual instruction samples.
Gating maps show traversal concentrates in shallow layers; at inference traversal is applied only to user-question tokens to limit latency.

title: NeuralSolver: Learning Algorithms For Consistent and Efficient Extrapolation Across General Tasks
relevance_reason: Recurrent-depth solver (single-layer conv-LSTM iterated with input recall) for easy-to-hard extrapolation, extending Deep Thinking to different-size tasks.
one_sentence: Iterates a layer-normalized convolutional LSTM with input recall, then aggregates with max-pooling, trained with a multi-size curriculum; extrapolates from small to much larger mazes, prefix sums, chess and RL grid tasks with far fewer parameters than DT-Recall.
key_contributions: Recurrent module = one conv-LSTM layer with layer norm and recall of the input at every iteration; processing module with optional global max-pool for different-size tasks.
Curriculum over multiple small training sizes; new different-size benchmark (1S-Maze, GoTo, Pong, Doorkey).
Reports no overthinking without progressive loss; gated recurrence beats recurrent ResNet block in ablation.

Gating in the recurrent cell substitutes for progressive loss to avoid overthinking, consistent with gated-recurrence findings elsewhere (Conv-LiGRU, 2502.10954). The corpus also contains 't:neuralthink algorithm synthesis that extrapolates in general tasks', possibly the same work under an earlier title (not verified).

title: Adaptive recurrent vision performs zero-shot computation scaling to unseen difficulty levels
relevance_reason: Convolutional RNNs iterated on static images with ACT-style learned halting; test-time iteration count scales with difficulty for zero-shot extrapolation.
one_sentence: Combines ConvRNNs (ConvGRU and a biologically inspired LocRNN) with ACT halting on PathFinder and Mazes; halting steps grow with difficulty and the models extrapolate to harder unseen levels by iterating longer, while a weight-tied R-ResNet fails to learn.
key_contributions: AdRNNs: ConvRNN + Graves-style learned halting with ponder cost on static visual reasoning tasks.
Halting step correlates with difficulty (contour length, maze route length) and increases beyond training range at test time.
Learned halting beats stability-based halting (hConvGRU) on extrapolation; ungated weight-tied R-ResNet-30 fails to learn.

claims.evidence_quote: The simpler recurrent network without gating, weight-tied R-ResNet-30, was unable to learn on PathFinder and on Mazes highlighting the importance of specialized operations such as gating and backpropagation through time.

claims.claim: Learned ACT halting outperforms halting based on hidden-state stability; stability halting fails entirely on PathFinder-21/24.
claims.evidence_quote: AdRNNs perform better than hConvGRU (stable halting) on both datasets; especially, stable halting completely fails to show generalization to PathFinder-21 and -24.

Supports gating as important for stable recurrence (also NeuralSolver 2402.15393).

key: t:iterative convergent computation may not be a useful inductive bias for residual neural networks
title: Iterative convergent computation may not be a useful inductive bias for residual neural networks
relevance_reason: Interpolates between ResNets and weight-tied recurrent ResNets via soft gradient coupling and tests whether iterative convergent computation helps.
one_sentence: Defines indices of iteration and convergence, finds ordinary ResNets do not learn iterative solutions, and shows that soft weight sharing (gradient coupling) and spectral-norm Lipschitz constraints make ResNets iterative and convergent but do not improve accuracy.
key_contributions: Three indices quantifying iterative convergence in residual networks.
Soft gradient coupling as recurrence regularization that interpolates between a ResNet and a fully weight-tied recurrent ResNet; spectral normalization for convergence.
Negative result: neither regularizer improves accuracy on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 or Digitclutter.

setup.benchmarks: classification accuracy on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Digitclutter

claims.claim: Conventionally trained ResNets can express but do not learn iterative solutions.
claims.evidence_quote: Consistent with previous work, we show that, even though ResNets can express iterative solutions, they do not learn them when trained conventionally on computer vision tasks.

claims.claim: Encouraging weight sharing (toward a recurrent ResNet) and convergence does not improve classification accuracy, including on occlusion tasks.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (same depth, varying degree of weight sharing); exact matching not stated in abstract
claims.evidence_quote: However, neither recurrence regularization nor spectral normalization improve classification accuracy on standard visual recognition tasks (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100) or on challenging recognition tasks with partial occlusions (Digitclutter).

limitations: Abstract only; small vision benchmarks; architecture sizes not stated in abstract.
venue: bioRxiv (corpus metadata, doi 10.1101/2023.10.13.562196)
survey_notes: Lineage / mechanisms. A rare clean negative result: making ResNets more recurrent (soft tying) and convergent gives no accuracy gain on recognition tasks, consistent with Liao and Poggio (1604.03640) that tied ResNets match but do not beat untied ones, and contrasting with algorithmic tasks where recurrence helps extrapolation (Deep Thinking line). Supports the survey point that recurrence pays off on iterative/algorithmic problems more than on perception.

title: Dynamic Recursive Neural Network
relevance_reason: Reuses CNN blocks recursively with per-block gates deciding loop counts; loop-specific batch norm to stabilize training.
one_sentence: Replaces duplicated building blocks of deep CNNs with recursively applied blocks whose gates adaptively choose loop counts, using Loopy Variable Batch Normalization; fewer parameters and compute with higher accuracy on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k.
key_contributions: Block-level recursion: fewer unique blocks applied repeatedly.
Per-block gate that adaptively decides how many times each recursive block loops.
Loopy Variable Batch Normalization (per-loop statistics), corrected for gate-induced statistical bias.

setup.benchmarks: CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1k accuracy

claims.claim: Recursive blocks with adaptive loop gates reduce parameters and compute while outperforming the original model.
claims.regime: unclear (fewer parameters and compute than the original; abstract only)
claims.evidence_quote: Experiments show that the DRNN reduces the parameters and computational cost and while outperforms the original model in term of the accuracy consistently on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k.

claims.claim: Recursive networks are hard to train; per-loop batch normalization stabilizes gradients.
claims.evidence_quote: Since the recursive networks are hard to train, we propose the Loopy Variable Batch Normalization (LVBN) to stabilize the volatile gradient.

limitations: Abstract only.
venue: CVPR 2019 (corpus metadata, doi 10.1109/CVPR.2019.00529)
survey_notes: Lineage / adaptive depth: early per-block recursion with learned loop gates and loop-indexed normalization, a precursor of loop-index-specific normalization or step embeddings in looped Transformers and of per-layer adaptive depth (e.g., MoR).

key: t:deep equilibrium object detection and segmentation
title: Deep Equilibrium Object Detection and Segmentation
relevance_reason: Query-decoder refinement modeled as the fixed point of a weight-tied implicit (DEQ) layer for detection and instance segmentation; journal extension of 2308.09564.
one_sentence: DEQ-Decoder treats query refinement as fixed-point solving with a two-step unrolled equilibrium, refinement-aware inexact gradients (RAG) and perturbed deep supervision (RAP); DEQDet beats AdaMixer with faster convergence and less memory, and DEQSeg extends it to instance segmentation.
key_contributions: Infinite-refinement query decoder via a DEQ layer with a two-step unrolled equilibrium equation.
Refinement-aware gradient (RAG) and refinement-aware perturbation deep supervision (RAP) for stable training.
Extension from detection (DEQDet) to instance segmentation (DEQSeg).

setup.model_sizes: ResNet50 backbone, 300 queries
setup.benchmarks: MS COCO mAP, AP_s; instance segmentation box and mask mAP

claims.claim: The DEQ decoder converges faster, uses less memory and outperforms the explicit multi-layer AdaMixer decoder.
claims.evidence_quote: DEQDet converges faster, consumes less memory, and achieves better results than the baseline counterpart (AdaMixer).

survey_notes: Beyond-language (vision). Not a duplicate of 2308.09564 but its journal extension (adds instance segmentation, RAG/RAP). Example of looping only a component (the query decoder) rather than the backbone.

key: t:deep equilibrium non autoregressive sequence learning
title: Deep Equilibrium Non-Autoregressive Sequence Learning
relevance_reason: Casts non-autoregressive decoder refinement as a dynamical system and solves its fixed point with a DEQ (weight-tied, infinite-depth) for machine translation.
one_sentence: Treats NAR translation models as iterative refinement z = f(z, x) and solves directly for the equilibrium with black-box root finding and implicit differentiation, consistently improving several strong NAR backbones on four WMT benchmarks.
key_contributions: View of NAR sequence generation as a dynamical system whose optimal prediction is its equilibrium.
DEQNAR: root-finding solvers plus implicit differentiation with constant memory on top of NAR backbones.
Consistent gains across several NAR backbones on four WMT translation benchmarks.

setup.benchmarks: WMT translation (four benchmarks)

claims.claim: Solving for the equilibrium of the NAR refinement dynamics yields more accurate predictions and helps several NAR backbones.
claims.regime: unclear (abstract; likely same backbone parameters, more compute)

limitations: Abstract only; compute cost of root finding not stated in abstract.
venue: Findings of ACL 2023 (corpus metadata, doi 10.18653/v1/2023.findings-acl.747)
survey_notes: Lineage / language: an early fixed-point (DEQ) language-generation model, connecting looped refinement to non-autoregressive and diffusion-style LMs. Belongs with DEQ language models (Bai et al.) in the equilibrium branch of the design space.

key: t:weight tied adaptive recursive vision language action transformer for efficient multimodal robotic control

one_sentence: Recursive VLA architecture: pretrained vision-language encoders plus gated fusion feed a weight-tied Transformer iterated for variable depth; on DROID it reports 82.4% lower action MSE than a non-recursive baseline at 1.5x inference cost.
key_contributions: Weight-tied recursive Transformer refinement of fused vision, language and proprioceptive features for continuous action prediction.
Variable-depth reasoning without increasing model size.
Evaluation on the DROID manipulation dataset with action MSE and tolerance accuracy.

title: One Wide Feedforward is All You Need
relevance_reason: Component-level cross-layer sharing: one FFN shared by all encoder layers, decoder FFNs removed; attention stays untied, so the network is not a loop of a full block.
one_sentence: In encoder-decoder MT Transformers, sharing one FFN across encoder layers and dropping decoder FFNs costs little BLEU; widening the shared FFN back to the original parameter count beats Transformer Big in accuracy and decoding speed.
key_contributions: Systematic sharing/dropping of FFNs across encoder and decoder layers (SharedEnc, SharedDec, SharedEncDec, NoDec).
One Wide FFN: a single shared encoder FFN with d_ff' = (N_enc + N_dec) x d_ff, no decoder FFN, at the same total parameters as Transformer Big.
CKA analysis showing representations stay similar to the baseline when sharing FFNs; sharing attention instead causes larger drops.

title: Learning Graph Algorithms With Recurrent Graph Neural Networks
relevance_reason: Weight-tied recurrent message-passing layer iterated a variable number of rounds to extrapolate graph algorithms from small to much larger graphs.
one_sentence: Recurrent GNNs trained on 10-node graphs extrapolate to graphs up to 1000x larger when using skip connections to the input, L2 state regularization and edge convolutions; a non-recurrent 10-layer GIN cannot extrapolate.
key_contributions: Identifies three techniques for recurrent GNN extrapolation: input skip connections (recall), L2 regularization of node states, edge convolutions.
Stability test: predictions stay correct from 10 up to 10,000 recurrent rounds only with state regularization.
Learned behavior resembles dead-end filling (path finding) and BFS (distance).

setup.train_tokens_or_data: algorithmic graph datasets (prefix sum, distance, path finding), training graphs of size 10
setup.loops_test: up to 10,000 rounds; more rounds for larger graphs
setup.baselines: non-recurrent GIN with 10 separate convolutions, IterGNN
setup.benchmarks: F1 on graphs up to 1000x larger than training

claims.claim: Recurrent GNNs extrapolate to graphs up to 1000x larger than training, beating IterGNN; a non-recurrent GIN fails beyond training sizes.
claims.regime: iso_data (all trained on size-10 graphs); non-recurrent GIN has 10 distinct layers (iso_effective_depth at training depth)
claims.evidence_quote: Both the RecGIN-E and RecGRU-E can extrapolate to graphs that are up to 1000 times larger than the graphs encountered during training, with the GRU variant achieving the best results overall.

claims.claim: Input skip connections are necessary for extrapolation, confirming Deep Thinking's recall finding for GNNs.
claims.evidence_quote: This confirms the findings of Schwarzschild et al., that access to the input features is a crucial part of gaining extrapolation abilities.

claims.claim: Without state regularization accuracy collapses after about 100 rounds; with L2 regularization predictions stay stable for many more rounds.
claims.evidence_quote: Afterwards, the models trained with L2 regularization still stay stable while accuracy declines rapidly without regularization.

survey_notes: Beyond-language (graphs) and lineage of easy-to-hard extrapolation. Input injection (recall) and state regularization are the graph analogues of input injection and normalization in looped Transformers. Stability over 10,000 rounds parallels the overthinking problem of 2202.05826.

title: EdgeFormer: A Parameter-Efficient Transformer for On-Device Seq2seq Generation
relevance_reason: Encoder layers share weights (each parameter used 6 times) with layer-specific adaptation (bias, LoRA, prefix) under a 10M parameter budget; compares directly against Universal Transformer.
one_sentence: On-device seq2seq Transformer (under 10M params) that shares encoder FFN and attention parameters across layers with balanced reuse load, plus per-layer Bias/LoRA/Prefix adaptation; beats Universal Transformer at similar size and FLOPs on WMT14 En-De.
key_contributions: Encoder-favored and load-balanced parameterization principles: reuse parameters moderately (diminishing returns when overused), and spend parameters on the encoder rather than the decoder.
Layer adaptation for tied layers: Bias-LA, Adapter-LA (layer-specific LoRA), Prefix-LA (layer-specific prefix tokens).
Releases EdgeLM, a pretrained on-device seq2seq model.

claims.evidence_quote: moderately reusing parameters (e.g., when x ≤ 4) helps better utilize the parameters, resulting in significant performance gain without increasing parameters.

title: Compact and Optimal Deep Learning with Recurrent Parameter Generators
relevance_reason: Decouples architecture depth from degrees of freedom by generating every layer's weights from one shared parameter ring with fixed random permutations and sign flips; not looping one block, but the same parameters-vs-depth decoupling.
one_sentence: A recurrent parameter generator fills all layers of a large network from a small shared ring of free parameters using random permutations and sign flips; ResNet18 keeps 96% of its ImageNet accuracy at 18% DoF and accuracy follows a log-linear law in DoF.
key_contributions: Recurrent parameter generator: one global model ring of free parameters, re-fetched for each layer with pre-generated random permutation and sign reflection (fixed random orthogonal transforms) to decorrelate shared weights.
Empirical log-linear / power-law relationship between degrees of freedom and accuracy, separate from architecture.
At the same DoF, deeper generated networks (ResNet34-RPG) beat shallower ones, and RPG beats MDEQ with much lower inference time.

setup.model_sizes: ResNet18/34 backbones with DoF from about 8K-36K up to 11M; ViT-RPG
setup.baselines: ResNet-vanilla at matched DoF, MDEQ, pruning and weight-sharing compression methods (deep compression, hashing trick, Lego filters)
setup.benchmarks: top-1 accuracy, inference time

claims.claim: At the same number of free parameters, RPG networks beat vanilla ResNets, and the deeper ResNet34-RPG beats ResNet18-RPG, i.e., more compute per parameter helps.
claims.evidence_quote: ResNet34-RPG achieves higher accuracy than ResNet18RPG, indicating increasing time complexity gives performance gain.

claims.claim: Reusing the MDEQ multiscale block 2-4 times at the same DoF beats MDEQ's fixed-point solution with 15-25x less inference time.
claims.regime: iso_param vs DEQ; inference compute lower for RPG
claims.evidence_quote: At the same number of model DoF, RPG achieves 3% - 6% performance gain with 15 - 25x less inference time.

claims.claim: A ResNet18 implemented with DoF of one conv layer still reaches 67.2% ImageNet top-1.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth vs ResNet18-vanilla (same architecture, fewer DoF)
claims.evidence_quote: a ResNet18 can be implemented with DoF equivalent to one convolution layer in a ResNet18-vanilla (4.72× DoF reduction) and still achieves 67.2% ImageNet top-1 accuracy.

numbers.quote: RPG achieves 96% of ResNet18's performance with only 18% DoF (the equivalent of one convolutional layer) and 52% of ResNet34's performance with only 0.25% DoF!
