survey_notes: Neighbors / design space (generated or permuted shared weights). Directly supports the survey thesis that parameters and depth are separable axes: at fixed DoF, deeper generated networks are better (iso-param depth scaling), with a log-linear DoF-accuracy law. Also a head-to-head where explicit reuse of a block 2-4 times beats a DEQ fixed point at the same DoF and far lower inference time.

title: RAFT: Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms for Optical Flow
relevance_reason: Weight-tied convolutional GRU update operator applied iteratively (12 in training, up to 200 at inference) to refine a flow field toward a fixed point.
one_sentence: Optical flow via a 2.7M-parameter tied ConvGRU update operator that iteratively looks up all-pairs correlation volumes; tied weights beat untied ones with 7x fewer parameters, and more inference updates than trained keep improving without divergence.
key_contributions: Iterative refinement with a single tied, lightweight update operator mimicking optimization steps, instead of untied cascades.
Unroll 12 updates in training but run an arbitrary number at inference (tested up to 200) without divergence.
State-of-the-art KITTI and Sintel results at the time, with fewer parameters and faster training.

setup.model_sizes: full model 4.8M parameters; update operator 2.7M
setup.benchmarks: Sintel clean/final EPE, KITTI-15 F1-epe/F1-all

claims.claim: Tying the update operator weights across iterations gives better accuracy than untied per-iteration weights, with far fewer parameters.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (same number of updates, tied vs untied), iso_data
claims.evidence_quote: Here, we test a version of our approach where each update operator learns a separate set of weights. Accuracy is better when weights are tied and the parameter count is significantly lower.

claims.claim: Trained with 12 unrolled updates, the model can run many more at inference, keeps improving, and does not diverge even at 200.
claims.evidence_quote: Our method quickly converges, surpassing PWC-Net after 3 updates and FlowNet2 after 6 updates, but continues to improve with more updates.

claims.claim: A gated (GRU) update block converges better than a plain 3-layer conv update.
claims.evidence_quote: We achieve better performance by using the GRU block, likely because the gated activation makes it easier for the sequence of flow estimates to converge.

numbers.what: tied vs untied: Sintel clean/final EPE, KITTI F1-epe/F1-all, params
numbers.quote: Tying Tied Weights Untied Weights 1.63 1.96 2.83 3.20 5.54 7.64 19.8 24.1 4.8M 32.5M

numbers.what: update operator size and iteration count vs IRR
numbers.quote: our update operator has only 2.7M parameters and can be applied 100+ times

numbers.what: Sintel final EPE
numbers.quote: On Sintel (final pass), RAFT obtains an end-point-error of 2.855 pixels, a 30% error reduction from the best published result (4.098 pixels).

survey_notes: Beyond-language (vision) and a clean iso-effective-depth data point: tied (4.8M) beats untied (32.5M) at the same number of updates, contrary to the usual LM finding that untied stacks win at equal depth. Explanation offered: the operator mimics optimization steps (an iterative-algorithm prior). Loop extrapolation (train 12, test up to 200) without divergence relies on bounded/gated activations and per-step supervision; compare to looped LMs that degrade beyond trained loop counts.

title: Recurrent Segmentation for Variable Computational Budgets
relevance_reason: Weight-shared convolutional LSTM stack iteratively updates a segmentation canvas on top of fixed ResNet features; iteration count sets the compute budget at inference.
one_sentence: A ConvLSTM refinement module additively updates segmentation logits each iteration from fixed ResNet features; running more iterations traces a speed-accuracy curve on PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes, and predictions keep improving past the trained six iterations.
key_contributions: Additive-canvas recurrent segmentation: each iteration feeds previous logits plus image features back into shared ConvLSTMs.
One trained model covers a range of compute budgets by varying iterations; each iteration costs under 7 GFLOPs.
Reuse of previous-frame segmentations for cheaper video segmentation.

setup.loops_train: 6 iterations, single loss at iteration six
setup.baselines: PSPNet, DeepLabV3 and other feed-forward segmenters
setup.benchmarks: mIOU (VOC, Cityscapes), iIOU, GFLOPs

claims.claim: Running the RNN for more iterations than trained keeps improving predictions.
claims.evidence_quote: Interestingly, if one runs the network for more steps than it was originally trained, the RNN predictions continue to improve (Figure 5, blue curves) as the canvas saturates.

claims.claim: Loss placement shapes the anytime curve: supervising early iterations helps early predictions but hurts the best result and breaks monotonic improvement.
claims.evidence_quote: applying the loss to iteration three or earlier improved the prediction quality at earlier iterations, but decreased the quality of the best segmentation

claims.claim: With many iterations, the RNN performs comparably to state-of-the-art feed-forward segmenters, but worse on high-spatial-frequency classes.
claims.evidence_quote: When run for many iterations, the RNN performs comparably to state-of-the-art networks [21, 69, 8, 72, 9], but performs notably worse on specific classes that have high spatial frequency features

numbers.what: compute of one pass at one iteration (513x513)
numbers.quote: A single inference pass of one image at a single iteration results in 61.1 GFLOPs of computation

numbers.what: marginal cost per extra iteration
numbers.quote: while each subsequent iteration only involves an additional pass through the RNN layers at a marginal cost of less than 7 GFLOPs.

limitations: Weaker on fine-structure classes (bicycle, chair).
survey_notes: Beyond-language (vision) / adaptive depth: early anytime recurrent refinement where iteration count is a deployment knob, with positive test-time extrapolation past the trained depth. The finding that supervising only the final iteration yields better peak quality and monotone anytime curves than earlier-iteration losses is relevant to deep-supervision design choices in looped LMs.

title: Bridging the Gaps Between Residual Learning, Recurrent Neural Networks and Visual Cortex
relevance_reason: Foundational observation that a shallow RNN unrolled in time equals a deep ResNet with weights shared across layers; tests weight-tied ResNets against untied ones.
one_sentence: Shows a ResNet with shared weights is a time-invariant RNN, introduces multi-state fully recurrent nets and time-specific batch norm, and finds weight-tied versions perform similarly to untied ResNets on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet with far fewer parameters.
key_contributions: Formal equivalence: shallow recurrent system unrolled in time = deep ResNet with weight sharing across layers.
Multi-state (multi-stage) recurrent generalization (FRNN) as a model of the ventral stream; error decreases as readout time (unrolling) increases at fixed parameters.
Time-specific batch normalization: per-step normalization statistics are needed; sharing BN statistics across time hurts.

setup.benchmarks: CIFAR-10 error, ImageNet top-1/top-5 error

claims.claim: A weight-shared (recurrent) ResNet with orders of magnitude fewer parameters performs similarly to the corresponding untied ResNet.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (same unrolled depth, shared vs non-shared)
claims.evidence_quote: A direct implementation of such a RNN, although having orders of magnitude fewer parameters, leads to a performance similar to the corresponding ResNet.

claims.claim: Sharing weights in the first stage always helps, while sharing in later stages sometimes slightly hurts.
claims.evidence_quote: sharing weights over time in the first stage of ResNet always improves performance. However, sharing weights in the later stages does sometimes slightly lower performance.

claims.claim: At fixed parameters, longer unrolling (readout time) consistently lowers error.
claims.evidence_quote: We observe in (D) and (E) that error reduces as t increases, while #param. is kept the same.

claims.claim: Batch-norm statistics must be time-specific in recurrent nets; sharing them across time hurts.
claims.evidence_quote: we found that it generally hurts performance when the normalization statistics (i.e., average, standard deviation) in batch normalization are shared across time.

limitations: Convergence not guaranteed as t grows; 4-state models computationally heavy; mainly CIFAR-10.
survey_notes: Lineage: canonical 'ResNet = unrolled RNN with tied weights' reference. Time-specific BN is an early instance of loop-indexed normalization (cf. DRNN LVBN, step embeddings in looped Transformers). Stage-dependent benefit of sharing (early yes, late sometimes no) parallels LM findings that some layers (first/last) should remain unique (prelude/coda).

title: Value Iteration Networks
relevance_reason: Planning module that applies one convolution + max-pool layer recurrently K times (tied weights) to emulate K steps of value iteration; includes a tied vs untied ablation.
one_sentence: Embeds a differentiable value-iteration module (a conv layer and channel max-pool applied K times with shared weights) in a policy network; VINs generalize to unseen grid-worlds and Mars terrain better than reactive CNNs, and untying the K layers hurts, especially with less data.
key_contributions: VI module: K recurrent applications of a convolution over reward and value maps plus max over action channels, trained end-to-end by backprop.
K chosen proportional to grid size so information can propagate from goal to all states (depth set by problem size).
Tied vs untied ablation: untied K-layer networks with more parameters degrade, more so in low-data regimes.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic grid-worlds (8x8 to 28x28), Mars overhead terrain images, continuous control, WebNav
setup.baselines: reactive CNN and FCN policies; VIN with untied weights
setup.benchmarks: success rate, trajectory length difference, prediction loss

claims.claim: Untying the weights of the K recurrent VI layers (same effective depth, more parameters) degrades performance, most at small training-data sizes.
claims.evidence_quote: Our results, in Table 2 show that untying the weights degrades performance, with a stronger effect for smaller sizes of training data.

claims.claim: VINs outperform reactive CNN/FCN policies on grid-worlds, with the gap growing with problem size.
claims.regime: unmatched (VIN has larger effective depth K)
claims.evidence_quote: For all domain sizes, VIN networks significantly outperform standard reactive networks. Note that the performance gap increases dramatically with problem size.

numbers.what: 16x16 grid-world success rate with 20% training data, tied vs untied VIN
numbers.quote: VIN Succ. rate 98.2% 99.4% 99.3% Traj. diff. 0.106 0.018 0.089 VIN Untied Weights Pred. Succ. Traj. loss rate diff. 0.09 91.9% 0.094

numbers.what: grid-world success rate VIN vs CNN (three domain sizes)
numbers.quote: VIN Success rate 99.6% 99.3% 97% Traj. diff. 0.001 0.089 0.086 Pred. loss 0.02 0.10 0.13 CNN Succ. rate 97.9% 87.6% 74.2%

limitations: Requires a planning MDP structure (local transitions as conv kernels); K fixed per domain.
venue: 30th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2016), Barcelona, Spain
builds_on: Ilin et al. cellular simultaneous recurrent networks
survey_notes: Lineage (algorithm-aligned recurrence) and beyond-language (RL/planning). Early iso-effective-depth evidence that tying helps when the loop matches an iterative algorithm, consistent with RAFT (2003.12039) and Deep Thinking. Depth chosen proportional to problem size anticipates easy-to-hard loop scaling.

title: Understanding Deep Architectures using a Recursive Convolutional Network
relevance_reason: Uses a convnet with weights tied across layers to separate the effects of number of layers (depth), feature maps (width) and parameters.
one_sentence: With a recursive (weight-tied) convnet, holding parameters fixed and adding layers improves CIFAR-10/SVHN accuracy, extra parameters at fixed depth help, and feature-map width matters little once parameters and depth are controlled.
key_contributions: Controlled design: tied vs untied convnets to vary layers, parameters and feature maps independently.
Depth alone (more tied layers at constant parameters) increases performance until overfitting at 8 layers on CIFAR-10.
At matched parameters and layers, tied (wider) and untied (narrower) models perform about the same: width is ancillary.

setup.model_sizes: M = 32-256 feature maps, L = 1-16 layers beyond the first (CIFAR-10); about 195K-parameter matched pairs
setup.baselines: untied convnets of same depth or same parameter count
setup.benchmarks: test/train classification error

claims.claim: At constant parameters (tied model), adding layers improves performance, because more nonlinearities allow more complex functions.
claims.evidence_quote: At these depths, therefore, adding more layers alone tends to increase performance, even though no additional parameters are introduced.

claims.claim: At the same depth and width, untied models (more parameters) beat tied ones, with the gap closing for the largest models.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (tied vs untied, same M and L)
claims.evidence_quote: Since the points fall below the y = x line, classification performance is better for the untied model than it is for the tied.

claims.claim: At matched parameters and depth, tied and untied models perform about the same despite different widths, so performance is set by parameters and layers.
claims.evidence_quote: perform about the same in each case. Thus, performance is determined by the number of parameters and layers, and is insensitive to the number of feature maps.

numbers.what: example matched pair (untied L=3, M=71 vs tied L=3, M=108)
numbers.quote: an untied model with L = 3 layers and M = 71 feature maps has P = 195473 parameters, while a tied model with L = 3 layers and M = 108 feature maps has P = 195058 parameters

limitations: Small convnets on CIFAR-10/SVHN; authors note caveats of the special tied architecture; overfitting at 8+ layers.
survey_notes: Lineage (earliest controlled depth-vs-parameters disentanglement with tied layers). Directly supports the survey thesis: depth (applications of shared weights) is a separate axis from parameters; also gives the canonical iso-effective-depth result that untied beats tied at equal depth (contrast RAFT 2003.12039 and VIN 1602.02867 where tied wins on algorithm-like tasks).

title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
relevance_reason: Layer deletion/swap interventions on pretrained (non-looped) LLMs that motivate the iterative-inference view and the prelude/core/coda split used by looped designs.
one_sentence: Deleting or swapping adjacent layers in Pythia, GPT-2, Phi, Qwen 2.5 and LLaMA 3.2 retains 72-95% of top-1 predictions; early and final layers are fragile, middle layers robust, motivating four stages (detokenization, feature engineering, prediction ensembling, residual sharpening).
key_contributions: Systematic layer drop and adjacent-swap interventions across five model families without fine-tuning.
Localized sensitivity: first-layer interventions are catastrophic; middle layers robust; swapping less harmful than dropping.
Four-stage hypothesis of depth-dependent computation, supported by mechanistic evidence.

setup.model_sizes: Pythia 410M-6.9B, GPT-2 family, Phi-1/1.5/2, Qwen 2.5, LLaMA 3.2
setup.benchmarks: KL divergence, relative top-1 accuracy, HellaSwag, ARC-Easy, LAMBADA

claims.claim: Without fine-tuning, models keep 72-95% of their top-1 predictions after deleting or swapping adjacent layers.
claims.evidence_quote: Surprisingly, models retain 72–95% of their original top-1 prediction accuracy without any fine-tuning.

claims.claim: Middle layers are robust to deletion and reordering, and swapping adjacent layers is less harmful than dropping them; first-layer interventions are catastrophic.
claims.evidence_quote: In contrast to the first and last layer interventions, the middle layers are remarkably robust to both deletion and minor order changes.

limitations: Interventions only; stage boundaries are a hypothesis; no repetition of layers tested here.
survey_notes: Mechanisms section: evidence for iterative refinement in middle layers and distinct early/late stages, which motivates looping middle blocks and keeping unique prelude/coda layers (Huginn-style sandwich, retrofit methods that loop middle layers). Does not test layer repetition; Layers as Painters (2407.09298) shows naive single-layer repetition is catastrophic, so robustness to deletion does not imply tolerance to repeating.

title: When Do Early-Exit Networks Generalize? A PAC-Bayesian Theory of Adaptive Depth
relevance_reason: Generalization theory for adaptive-depth (early-exit) networks, depending on expected exit depth and exit-depth entropy; applies in principle to halting in looped models but is not about weight sharing.
one_sentence: PAC-Bayesian bounds for early-exit networks that scale with expected exit depth and exit-depth entropy rather than maximum depth, with sufficient conditions for adaptive depth to generalize better than fixed depth; bounds are 1.52-3.87x of observed gaps.
key_contributions: Generalization bound with sample complexity O((E[D] d + H(D))/eps^2) instead of depending on maximum depth K.
Sufficient conditions under which adaptive-depth networks strictly beat fixed-depth ones; extension to approximately label-independent (learned) routing.
Validation on 6 architectures / 7 benchmarks incl. GPT-2-small with CALM-style exits; bound-guided thresholds match validation tuning within 0.1-0.3%.

setup.model_sizes: MSDNet, ResNet-56, EfficientNet-B0, GPT-2-small (12 exits) and others
setup.baselines: classical VC / information-theoretic bounds; validation-tuned thresholds
setup.benchmarks: bound tightness ratio, generalization gap

claims.claim: Generalization of adaptive-depth networks is governed by expected exit depth and exit-depth entropy, not maximum depth.
claims.evidence_quote: We prove the first generalization bounds depending on exit-depth entropy H(D) and expected depth E[D] rather than maximum depth K

claims.claim: Bounds are much tighter than classical bounds, and bound-guided exit thresholds nearly match validation-tuned ones.
claims.evidence_quote: Experiments across 6 architectures on 7 benchmarks demonstrate tightness ratios of 1.52–3.87× (all p < 0.001) versus >100× for classical bounds.

limitations: 1.5-4x tightness gap; only up to ImageNet-100 and GPT-2-small; label-dependent routing degrades guarantees as eps*K grows.
survey_notes: Theory / adaptive depth: the bound's dependence on E[D] and H(D) is a candidate theoretical lens for learned halting in looped models (Ouro, PonderLM), but the analysis treats exits on a standard (untied) network and relies on (approximate) label independence of the exit policy; weight sharing across depths is not modeled.

title: Constant Bit-size Transformers Are Turing Complete
relevance_reason: Expressivity theory for CoT transformers with fixed size and precision; the scaling resource is context length (generated tokens), the alternative axis to looped depth.
one_sentence: Proves any Turing machine can be simulated by a constant bit-size (fixed precision and parameters) transformer generating CoT, provided the context window is long enough, and that window length s(n) characterizes exactly SPACE[s(n)].
key_contributions: Turing completeness without growing precision or embedding dimension, via simulation of Post machines (queue automata).
Theorem 1: WINDOW[s(n)] = SPACE[s(n)]; in particular polynomial windows give PSPACE.
Context window needs to scale with space, not time, complexity; O(s(n)) CoT tokens per TM step.

setup.model_sizes: constant bit-size (theory)
setup.baselines: prior Turing-completeness constructions (Perez et al., Merrill and Sabharwal, Li et al., PENCIL)

claims.claim: A constant bit-size transformer with a sufficiently long context window simulates any Turing machine, so longer inputs require only a longer window, not more parameters or precision.
claims.evidence_quote: We prove that any Turing machine running on inputs of arbitrary length can be simulated by a constant bit-size transformer, as long as the context window is sufficiently long.

claims.claim: The expressive power of a constant bit-size transformer with window s(n) is exactly SPACE[s(n)].
claims.evidence_quote: Theorem 1. For any non-decreasing function 𝑠 (𝑛) ≥ 𝑛, we have WINDOW [𝑠 (𝑛)] = SPACE [𝑠 (𝑛)]. In particular, WINDOW [ poly (𝑛)] = PSPACE.

limitations: Constructions use specific architectural modifications (Appendix A); expressivity only, no learnability.
survey_notes: Theory section, counterpart to looped-depth expressivity: here generated tokens (context) are the unbounded resource for a fixed-size model; looped models instead spend depth with bounded memory. Useful to frame the survey's 'third axis' argument: CoT scales with space via tokens, looping scales per-token depth (which alone does not give unbounded memory).

title: A Little Depth Goes a Long Way: The Expressive Power of Log-Depth Transformers
relevance_reason: Expressivity theory of (s, r, t)-universal (looped) transformers whose middle block is repeated Theta(log n) times; compares depth vs width vs CoT scaling.
one_sentence: Proves uniform looped transformers with depth Theta(log n) recognize regular languages and solve graph connectivity (beyond fixed-depth TC0 under standard conjectures), and that growing depth is more efficient than growing width or CoT; A5 experiments match the predicted log-depth law.
key_contributions: (s, r, t)-universal transformer formalism: s initial layers, r repeated layers unrolled to depth d(n) = ceil(log n), t final layers.
Theorems: log-depth suffices for regular language recognition and graph connectivity; width must grow superpolynomially and CoT steps superlogarithmically for the same problems.
Experiments on A5 state tracking: effective context length grows exponentially with depth (r^2 = 0.93), about 4.8 layers per log token.

setup.model_sizes: width 512 for depth sweeps; depth 6 for width sweeps
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 100 million A5 sequences of length up to 1024 with curriculum
setup.benchmarks: A5 state tracking effective context length n* (95% accuracy)

claims.claim: Looped transformers whose middle layers repeat Theta(log n) times can recognize regular languages and solve graph connectivity, which fixed-depth transformers cannot under standard conjectures.
claims.evidence_quote: We prove that even such highly uniform transformers, when allowed log-depth, can recognize regular languages2 and solve graph connectivity, two important reasoning problems known to be beyond fixed-depth transformers

claims.claim: Scaling depth is more efficient than scaling width (superpolynomial) or CoT steps (superlogarithmic) for these problems.
claims.evidence_quote: showed that scaling depth to solve these problems is more efficient than scaling width (which requires superpolynomial increase) or scaling chain-of-thought steps (which requires superlogarithmic increase).

claims.claim: Empirically (with non-looped transformers), effective A5 context length grows exponentially in depth with about 4.8 layers per log token, between the theoretical coefficients for universal (8) and non-uniform (4) transformers.
claims.evidence_quote: The empirical slope for the depth relationship is is 4.8 layers per log tokens. This is less than the slope of 8 derived for universal transformers in Theorem 1

claims.claim: Log depth cannot solve P-complete problems unless NC = P.
claims.evidence_quote: Unless NC = P, log-depth (or even polylog-depth) transformers cannot express P-complete problems including solving linear equalities

numbers.what: fit of depth vs log effective context length; width vs n*
numbers.quote: there is a very strong positive correlation (r2 = 0.93) between model depth (x-axis) and log n∗ (y-axis, log scale)

numbers.what: implied input-size limits at depth 32 and 80
numbers.quote: with a depth of only 32, such as in LLaMA 3.1 7B (Meta AI, 2024) and OLMo 7B (Ai2, 2024), transformers can recognize regular languages up to strings of length 107

limitations: Experiments used non-looped transformers; inductive biases and learning dynamics of looped models not analyzed; log depth does not reach P-complete problems.
venue: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
survey_notes: Theory section anchor: formal case that looped depth growing as log n is the most efficient of the three axes (depth, width, CoT) for state tracking and connectivity, supporting the 'third scaling axis' thesis. Caveat for the survey: the empirical confirmation uses untied transformers, so the loop-specific claim is theoretical only; the (s, r, t) formalism matches the prelude-core-coda design. Note the stated input length 107 is likely pdftotext rendering of a superscript (10^7); quote shows '107'.

title: TIDE: Token-Informed Depth Execution for Per-Token Early Exit in LLM Inference
relevance_reason: Post-training per-token early exit for standard (non-looped) LLMs via learned convergence routers; relevant to per-token halting and systems for adaptive depth.
one_sentence: Attaches tiny MLP routers at checkpoint layers of frozen LLMs, trained to predict when a token's hidden state has converged to the final layer, and reads logits from the earliest converged layer; reports single-digit percent throughput gains on 8B models.
key_contributions: Router calibration on 2,000 WikiText samples (under 3 minutes, about 4 MB checkpoint) using cosine similarity to the final hidden state as label.
Fused CUDA kernels for norm + routing and token compaction; works across HuggingFace causal LMs.
Post-hoc decode mode that keeps the KV cache fully populated by running all layers.

setup.model_sizes: DeepSeek R1 Distill 8B (32 layers), Qwen3 8B (36 layers)
setup.benchmarks: prefill latency, throughput, exit rates, one multi-step math problem for quality

claims.claim: On DeepSeek R1 Distill 8B, TIDE cuts prefill latency 7.2% and raises single-batch throughput 6.6%; on Qwen3 8B throughput rises 8.1% at batch size 8.
claims.regime: not_applicable (same model with and without exit)
claims.evidence_quote: reduces prefill latency by 7.2%, and increases single-batch throughput by 6.6%.

claims.claim: In decoding, the post-hoc mode runs all layers and only selects which layer's output to use, so it gives no wall-clock layer skipping.
claims.evidence_quote: T IDE's post-hoc mode runs all layers on every step, selecting only which layer's output to use. This produces correct results and preserves the KV cache, but does not achieve wall-clock layer skipping.

numbers.what: prefill exit distribution on DeepSeek R1 Distill 8B
numbers.value: 5% exit at layer 11, rest at layer 31
numbers.quote: T IDE achieves 100% prefill exit rate (5% of tokens exit at layer 11, the remaining at layer 31)

limitations: Decode mode does not skip compute; conservative threshold concentrates exits at the penultimate checkpoint; quality checked on a single math problem; negative throughput at batch 8 for DeepSeek R1.
survey_notes: Neighbors / systems: per-token exit for non-looped LLMs. Weak evidence (single-problem quality check, 'exit' in decoding saves no compute). The KV-cache problem it sidesteps (exited tokens leave later-layer KV missing) is the same issue looped models face with per-token loop counts; cite as illustration of that systems constraint rather than as a speedup result.

title: Dynamic Rebatching for Efficient Early-Exit Inference with DREX
relevance_reason: Serving system for early-exit LLMs (non-looped) addressing batching and missing-KV problems that equally affect per-token adaptive loop counts.
one_sentence: Dynamic Rebatching regroups requests at each exit point so exiting tokens finish immediately and continuing ones are batched for deeper layers, with copy-free buffers and virtual-memory KV sharing for skipped layers; 2-12% throughput gain with zero involuntary exits.
key_contributions: Shows grouped (batch-consensus) exit policies cause involuntary stays (lost speedup) or involuntary exits (quality loss); batched early exit gives under 2% gains in existing frameworks.
Copy-free rebatching buffer via virtual tensor indexing and an SLA-aware scheduler predicting rebatching profitability.
Missing KV for skipped layers handled by mapping skipped layers' entries to the same physical memory (state copying without duplication).

setup.model_sizes: Llama-EE models incl. Llama2-13B EE and Llama-EE-70B
setup.baselines: EE-LLM, Apparate, Miao et al., grouped exit policies (consensus, greedy)
setup.benchmarks: HELM text summarization; throughput; P95 confidence score; CUDA memory

claims.claim: Existing EE methods give large speedups without batching but marginal or negative gains with batching.
claims.evidence_quote: Early Exiting (EE) provides a significant throughput boost of up to 33% for non-batched inference on SOTA frameworks

claims.claim: DREX improves throughput 2-12% over baselines while eliminating involuntary exits and maintaining quality.
claims.evidence_quote: Our evaluation shows that DREX improves throughput by 2-12% compared to baseline approaches while maintaining output quality.

numbers.what: CUDA memory reduction from shared physical KV blocks for skipped layers
numbers.quote: reducing CUDA memory usage by as much as 18.3% compared to a traditional LLM.

limitations: Applies to early-exit (untied) LLMs; quality measured via confidence score on summarization.
survey_notes: Systems section: the batching mismatch (tokens in a batch want different depths) and the skipped-layer KV problem are directly the obstacles for per-token adaptive loop counts in looped LMs (e.g., MoR, Ouro halting); DREX's rebatching and KV-sharing via virtual memory are transferable solutions. Looped models have an advantage here: shared weights mean all depths use the same kernel, which may simplify rebatching (not tested in this paper).

title: Learning to Ponder: Adaptive Reasoning in Latent Space
relevance_reason: Latent 'pondering' by repeatedly adding a steering vector to frozen hidden states with an RL-trained halting controller; adaptive latent compute but no reuse of layers.
one_sentence: A sub-1M-parameter controller trained with GRPO decides, per input, how many additive steering-vector updates z_{k+1} = z_k + alpha_k h_steer to apply to a frozen LLM's hidden state before halting, cutting generated tokens 30-40% on GSM8K/MATH500 with equal or better accuracy.
key_contributions: Steering vector extracted from contrastive deliberative vs direct prompts, applied with exponentially decaying scale.
Halting controller (<=1M params) trained with GRPO on a reward combining accuracy and a FLOPs penalty, with curriculum.
Learned number of ponder steps correlates with problem difficulty.

setup.model_sizes: LLaMA-3-8B/70B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-0.5B/3B/7B-Instruct (frozen)
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA accuracy, tokens, FLOPs

claims.claim: FR-Ponder variants improve GSM8K accuracy by 3-5 points over CoT and Direct while using fewer tokens.
claims.regime: unclear (same frozen backbone; compute lower for FR-Ponder)
claims.evidence_quote: On GSM8K, FR-P ONDER variants improve accuracy by 3–5 points over standard CoT and Direct baselines, with FP-BoN and FP-Direct delivering the strongest gains.

claims.claim: Token usage falls 30-40% relative to CoT and BoN.
claims.evidence_quote: Across all model scales, FP-BoN and FP-Direct achieve the most pronounced reductions, often cutting token counts by 30–40% relative to standard CoT and BoN.

limitations: Pondering is an additive steering update, not extra layer computation; contributions list says 30-50% token reduction while results section says 30-40%.
survey_notes: Neighbors (latent adaptive compute without depth recurrence). Title says 'ponder' but no layers are re-applied, so it should not be counted as a looped model; useful only as an RL-trained halting controller example. Internal inconsistency on token reduction (30-50% vs 30-40%).

title: Not All LLM Reasoning is Visible in the Chain-of-Thought
relevance_reason: Safety evidence that frontier (non-looped) LLMs perform consequential computation in latent states via filler tokens, invisible to CoT monitors; motivates monitorability concerns for looped/latent reasoning.
one_sentence: Across 13 frontier models and three synthetic tasks, semantically irrelevant filler tokens improve accuracy by up to 13 points and let Claude Opus 4.5 satisfy a hidden constraint unseen by CoT monitors; activation probes detect what token monitors miss.
key_contributions: Defines and demonstrates invisible reasoning: filler-token computation that causally improves accuracy without interpretable output.
Hidden modular-arithmetic constraint satisfied via fillers, i.e., reasoning serving objectives invisible to CoT monitoring.
Activation patching and linear probing locate the useful signal in early layers and suggest activation-level monitors.

setup.model_sizes: 13 frontier models incl. Claude Opus 4.5, Qwen3-235B (94 layers), Gemini 3, GLM-5
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic reasoning tasks; RL and SFT on Qwen3-235B
setup.benchmarks: synthetic arithmetic, multiplication and constraint tasks

claims.claim: Many frontier models benefit from filler tokens, with accuracy gains up to 13 points depending on token type and model.
claims.evidence_quote: We evaluate 13 frontier language models across three tasks and find that many models benefit significantly from filler tokens, with accuracy improvements of up to 13 percentage points.

claims.claim: Neither RL nor SFT produced a filler-token benefit that persists at test time.
claims.evidence_quote: Reinforcement learning gives Qwen3-235B strong preferences over filler token content, but neither RL nor supervised fine-tuning produces a filler token benefit that persists at test time.

claims.claim: Patching early-layer activations recovers most of the filler-type performance gap, indicating the useful signal originates in early layers.
claims.evidence_quote: Patching at layers 0–30 recovers over 90% of the performance gap between the two filler types; patching at layers 70 and above yields negative recovery

limitations: Synthetic tasks; mechanism of filler computation not fully identified.
survey_notes: Safety section: supports the concern that latent computation (which looped models scale by design) escapes CoT monitoring; the paper itself names looped transformers (Geiping et al.) as a training direction motivated by the same prefill/decode efficiency incentives. Its activation-probe result suggests activation-level monitoring as a mitigation that would also apply to looped models.

title: How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?
relevance_reason: Transparency/monitorability study of a text-diffusion model that re-applies the whole network over T denoising steps with a continuous self-conditioning state; introduces opaque serial depth, a metric directly applicable to looped LMs.
one_sentence: Measures DiffusionGemma's opaque serial depth (serial computation between interpretable states) as 28.6x Gemma 4 if the inter-step bottleneck is opaque but 1.1x if it is mapped through interpretable tokens without loss; monitorability is similar to Gemma 4.
key_contributions: Decomposes transparency into variable transparency (interpretable intermediate states) and algorithmic transparency (reconstructing the process).

Opaque serial depth accounting: the denoising loop multiplies opaque depth by about T unless the inter-step state is interpretable; shows the bottleneck can be made interpretable without performance loss.
Case studies of diffusion-specific phenomena (non-chronological reasoning, token/sequence smearing) and monitorability evaluations.

setup.model_sizes: DiffusionGemma vs Gemma 4 26B A4B
setup.loops_test: T = 48 denoising steps worst case; 12 to 16 in practice with adaptive stopping
setup.benchmarks: opaque serial depth, Guan et al. 2025 monitorability evaluations

claims.claim: With an uninterpretable inter-step bottleneck, opaque serial depth is 28.6x the autoregressive Gemma 4; treating the bottleneck as interpretable reduces it to 1.1x.
claims.evidence_quote: if we assume that the bottleneck is interpretable, the empirical opaque serial depth upper bound drops to 23, 571 / 21, 235 = 1.1X that of Gemma 4 26B A4B

claims.claim: DiffusionGemma is similarly monitorable to Gemma 4, possibly because reasoning between canvases is autoregressive.
claims.evidence_quote: Our main result in Fig. 4 is that monitorability of DiffusionGemma is similar to the monitorability of Gemma.

numbers.what: opaque serial depth ratio with opaque bottleneck
numbers.quote: DiffusionGemma with an uninterpretable bottleneck is 608, 016 / 21, 235 = 28.6X larger than Gemma 4 26B A4B, the corresponding Gemma model.

limitations: Single model family; monitorability may be helped by multi-canvas autoregressive structure; T=48 is worst case.
survey_notes: Safety section: opaque serial depth is the right metric for looped LMs, whose per-token latent depth multiplies serial computation between interpretable (token) states by the loop count; unlike diffusion, looped models have no token bottleneck between loops, so the 1.1x mitigation does not obviously transfer (survey inference, not tested here). Pair with 2610.02741 (CoT monitorability of looped LMs) and 2607.22925.

title: PonderLM-3: Adaptive Token-Wise Pondering with Differentiable Masking
relevance_reason: Whole-model recurrence at a token position (last-layer hidden state fed back as input for K pondering steps) with a learned per-token router deciding how many steps to execute; compared head-to-head with LoopedLM and MoR at matched parameters and data.
one_sentence: Adds a router and differentiable attention mask to the PonderLM-2 latent-pondering backbone so each token executes only the useful pondering steps; at 70M/15B tokens it gives lower perplexity than LoopedLM, PonderLM-1/2 at matched executed steps, and at 410M matches PonderLM-2 with fewer FLOPs.
key_contributions: Token-wise step distribution from a lightweight router on the step-0 hidden state, realized as a differentiable attention mask in training and a matching hard pruning rule at inference (train-inference consistent).
Minimum-ponder penalty auxiliary loss; Jacobi-style parallel training of the recurrent pondering inherited from PonderLM-2.
Mechanism evidence: executed steps concentrate on intrinsically hard tokens; removing compute from easy tokens barely changes loss.

setup.model_sizes: 70M (Pareto and ablations), 410M (downstream)
setup.loops_train: max K in {2,3,4} pondering steps (K=3 default; ablation up to 5)
setup.baselines: PonderLM-1, PonderLM-2, LoopedLM (Giannou et al.; 4 loops), MoR (max 3 steps), Pause tokens (3)
setup.benchmarks: Pile PPL; LAMBADA, ARC-E/C, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, PIQA, SciQ, RACE

claims.claim: At matched executed additional steps (inference FLOPs proxy) and matched pretraining, PonderLM-3 has lower perplexity than fixed-depth PonderLM-1/2 and LoopedLM.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data, iso_infer_flop (executed steps as proxy)
claims.evidence_quote: Figure 3 shows that PonderLM-3 consistently defines a superior Pareto frontier, achieving the lowest perplexity at matched executed compute compared with the fixed-depth and looped baselines.

claims.claim: Downstream, PonderLM-3 is competitive with PonderLM-2 (not universally better) at lower inference compute.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data; inference FLOPs lower (8.86 vs 9.84 G/token)
claims.evidence_quote: Accordingly, Table 2 is not intended to claim universal wins; rather, it shows that our method maintains competitive accuracy under substantially reduced inference compute

claims.claim: Increasing the maximum number of pondering steps K from 2 to 5 consistently lowers pretraining loss, with diminishing returns.
claims.evidence_quote: Figure 6 shows that increasing 𝐾 consistently lowers pretraining cross-entropy in our setting, suggesting that additional pondering steps provide extra capacity for refining token representations.

numbers.what: estimated inference FLOPs (G/token) at 410M: LoopedLM 4 loops, Pause, MoR, PonderLM-1, PonderLM-2, PonderLM-3
numbers.quote: LoopedLM (4 loops) Pause (3 pauses) MoR (max 3 steps) PonderLM-1 (3 steps) PonderLM-2 (3 steps) PonderLM-3 (max 3 steps) 9.84 9.84 8.44 9.84 9.84 8.86

numbers.what: pretraining setup for Pareto comparison
numbers.quote: All models use a 70M-parameter LLaMA-style architecture and are pretrained on a 15B-token subset of The Pile Gao et al. [2020] with the same training hyperparameters.

limitations: Small scale (70M, 410M); inference FLOPs estimated via 6ND with executed steps, not measured wall-clock; downstream gains over PonderLM-2 not universal.
survey_notes: Adaptive depth / design space: token-level halting for whole-model latent recurrence, with one of the few matched (iso-param, iso-data, executed-compute-matched) comparisons against a looped LM and MoR. Note the recurrence passes the last-layer state back as an input embedding at extra positions (closer to Coconut-style latent tokens than to in-place block looping), so it straddles the looped-depth and latent-token categories. 'Inference FLOPs' are a 6ND proxy (with N parameters), which counts training-style FLOPs.

title: RRFC: Recursive Refinement via Feedback Conditioning for Iterative Image-to-Image Generation
relevance_reason: Re-applies an image-to-image generator to its own previous output fed back as extra input channels; output-level iteration rather than latent depth recurrence.
one_sentence: Feedback-conditioning wrapper that lets existing image-to-image generators revise their previous prediction over iterations; across 18 architecture-task settings it gives 7 significant improvements, 7 degradations and 4 null results.
key_contributions: Feed the most recent prediction back as auxiliary input channels to any generator (GAN, equilibrium, diffusion).
Evaluation over six baselines and three paired translation tasks with Holm-corrected tests.

claims.claim: Feedback refinement gives mixed results: as many significant degradations as improvements, with gains on reconstruction-fidelity tasks and losses on the semantic-layout task.
claims.regime: not_applicable (same generator with vs without feedback)
claims.evidence_quote: Across 18 architecture-task settings, RRFC yields seven Holm-corrected improvements, seven degradations, and four non-significant changes.

limitations: Gains only where the refinement objective overlaps the evaluated property.
survey_notes: Beyond-language (vision), output-space recurrence. Useful as a carefully controlled negative/mixed result: iterating a model on its own output does not reliably help.

title: BRAID: Learning Equilibrium Maps in Interdependent Security Games via Weight-Tied Iterative Graph Neural Networks
relevance_reason: Weight-tied GRU message-passing GNN unrolled K steps, mirroring damped best-response fixed-point dynamics, to amortize Nash equilibrium computation.
one_sentence: Weight-tied iterative GNN whose SUM aggregation and tied GRU update mirror best-response dynamics; maps game parameters to Nash equilibria up to 43x faster per instance and recovers equilibrium sensitivities.
key_contributions: Architecture derived from the best-response fixed point: tied GRU as a damped best-response step, parameter count independent of unroll depth K.
Interior-equilibrium training and input-noise regularization to improve sensitivity recovery without sensitivity labels.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic interdependent security games on networks (log-linear, quadratic-cost, log-CES utilities)

claims.claim: A single forward pass of the tied iterative GNN replaces iterative best-response computation, up to 43x faster per instance.
claims.evidence_quote: replacing iterative best response computation with a single forward pass that is up to 43X faster per instance.

numbers.what: per-instance speedup over best-response dynamics
numbers.quote: uses a weight-tied iterative graph neural network to learn a direct map from game parameters to Nash equilibrium effort profiles, replacing iterative best response computation with a single forward pass that is up to 43X faster per instance.

builds_on: DEQ (contrasted: BRAID unrolls instead of solving implicitly)
survey_notes: Beyond-language (graphs/economics): another case where the tied block is derived from a known fixed-point iteration (algorithm alignment), like VIN and RAFT.

title: Persistent Gaussian Perturbations Prevent Oversmoothing in Recurrent Graph Neural Networks
relevance_reason: Theory of a recurrent GNN that repeats one shared propagation step with injected noise; addresses representation collapse under many iterations.
one_sentence: Proves that injecting independent Gaussian noise after every step of a contractive recurrent GNN yields a geometrically ergodic chain whose stationary Dirichlet energy is bounded below, so representations cannot oversmooth.
key_contributions: Stochastic dynamical-system analysis of a noisy recurrent GNN under global contraction.
Explicit lower bound on stationary Dirichlet energy proportional to noise variance and graph spectral gap.

claims.claim: Persistent noise gives a positive lower bound on stationary Dirichlet energy, preventing asymptotic oversmoothing in deep recurrent message passing.
claims.evidence_quote: Our main theoretical result establishes an explicit positive lower bound on the expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to both the noise variance and the spectral gap of the underlying graph.

limitations: Requires a global contraction assumption; experiments are small numerical checks.
survey_notes: Theory / training stability: representation collapse under many iterations of a shared operator is the graph analogue of loop-collapse in looped LMs; stochastic perturbation per step relates to noise-injected or stochastic-depth looping.

title: Growing a Neural Network in Breadth, Depth, and Time
relevance_reason: Recurrent CNN on an infinite lattice with differentiable costs on breadth, depth and recurrent time steps; studies trade-offs among the three resources.
one_sentence: Optimizes differentiable breadth, depth and time costs jointly with task loss in a recurrent CNN; finds the three resources trade off for a given accuracy, networks take more recurrent steps on occluded inputs, and time correlates with human reaction times.
key_contributions: Differentiable resource costs for breadth, depth and recurrent time.
Emergent trade-offs and input-dependent time use.

claims.claim: Breadth, depth and recurrent time can be traded off against each other to reach a given accuracy, and networks spontaneously take more recurrent steps on occluded inputs.
claims.evidence_quote: We find that all three resources can be traded off against each other to achieve a given level of accuracy.

survey_notes: Lineage / neighbors: a normative version of the survey's thesis that width, depth and recurrent time are exchangeable resources; time adapts to input difficulty (occlusion), like adaptive-depth looped models.

title: Recurrent Sinusoidal INRs for Efficient High-Fidelity Representation
relevance_reason: A shared sinusoidal block iteratively refines the latent of an implicit neural representation for R steps, adding depth without parameters.
one_sentence: Shows sinusoidal recurrence enriches the harmonic spectral support of INRs; a shared sinusoidal block unrolled R steps beats feed-forward INRs with fewer parameters and optimization steps on images, and transfers to super-resolution, NeRF and SDF.
key_contributions: Spectral account: sinusoidal activations induce a harmonic line spectrum that recurrent unrolling broadens.
Comparison against feed-forward, non-sinusoidal recurrent and equilibrium-style sinusoidal INRs.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: RGB image fitting (e.g., Kodak24), super-resolution, NeRF, SDF
setup.baselines: feed-forward SIREN-style INRs, non-sinusoidal recurrent INRs, equilibrium-style sinusoidal models

claims.claim: At a fixed parameter budget, increasing recurrent unrolling steps from feed-forward to R=5 improves PSNR.
claims.evidence_quote: At optimization step 500, increasing the number of recurrent unrolling steps from a single feed-forward pass to R = 5 improves PSNR

numbers.what: PSNR at optimization step 500, feed-forward vs R=5 recurrent steps (same parameters)
numbers.quote: to R = 5 improves PSNR from 39.724 dB to 63.378 dB, with monotonic gains at every intermediate step under the same parameter count.

survey_notes: Beyond-language: clean iso-param depth-via-recurrence gain with a mechanistic (spectral) explanation of why repeated application of the same block adds capacity.

title: Listen, Think, Transcribe: Continuous Latent Test-Time Scaling for ASR
relevance_reason: Small adapter iteratively refines latent prefix positions on a frozen ASR decoder with a value head that halts the loop; latent test-time recurrence.
one_sentence: Adds a ~4M-parameter Latent Adapter that iteratively refines a few latent prefix positions of frozen Qwen3-ASR-0.6B plus a Value Head that halts; with 500 training utterances it lowers WER where fine-tuning, LoRA and prompt tuning regress.
key_contributions: Bounded, gated iterative latent updates on a frozen backbone (test-time latent scaling).
Value Head that predicts whether more computation helps and can skip the loop at entry.

setup.model_sizes: Qwen3-ASR-0.6B frozen, ~4M trainable
setup.benchmarks: FLEURS, VoxPopuli, ASCEND, 30 FLEURS languages

claims.claim: Under minimal data, LatentASR is the only tested adaptation method that reduces WER on both clean benchmarks; dynamic halting keeps most of the gain while skipping about half of utterances.
claims.regime: not_applicable (adaptation methods on same frozen backbone)
claims.evidence_quote: LatentASR is the only tested method that reduces WER on both clean benchmarks (FLEURS -2.54% and VoxPopuli -0.47% relative).

claims.claim: Forcing all loop steps overshoots: later updates can degrade the transcript, so early halting improves accuracy, not just cost; removing the bounded-delta update is catastrophic.
claims.evidence_quote: it truncates the loop before the still-active later steps degrade the transcript.

numbers.what: relative CER reduction on accented/code-switched ASCEND
numbers.quote: On accented and code-switched speech (ASCEND), LatentASR achieves a 16.0% relative CER reduction.

limitations: Small relative WER gains on clean speech; tiny training set.
survey_notes: Beyond-language (speech) and adaptive depth: latent test-time iteration retrofitted to a frozen model with learned halting; the gate truncates the loop before later steps degrade, a form of overthinking control.

title: Parallelized Hierarchical Connectome: A Spatiotemporal Recurrent Framework for Spiking State-Space Models
relevance_reason: Shared neuron and synapse layers iterated in a spatial loop within each timestep of an SSM, giving depth-independent parameter count; spiking/biological focus.
one_sentence: Turns temporal-only SSMs into spatiotemporal recurrent networks by iterating shared Neuron and Synapse layers in a Multi-Transmission Loop within each time window, with Theta(D^2) parameters instead of Theta(D^2 L); a spiking instantiation is competitive with 1,312-4,891 parameters.
key_contributions: Spatial recurrence within a timestep with shared layers (parameters independent of depth L).
Integration of five biological priors and microcontroller deployment.

setup.model_sizes: 1,312 to 4,891 trainable parameters

claims.claim: Iterating shared layers within each timestep makes parameter complexity Theta(D^2) versus Theta(D^2 L) for stacked SSMs, and the model is competitive with far larger SSM baselines.
claims.regime: unmatched (1-4 orders of magnitude fewer parameters)
claims.evidence_quote: achieving test accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art SSM baselines at 1,312 to 4,891 trainable parameters (1 to 4 orders of magnitude smaller than every baseline).

survey_notes: Neighbors / multi-timescale recurrence: an SSM analogue of hierarchical looping (depth recurrence nested inside time recurrence), relevant to hybrid looped + recurrent-sequence designs.

title: Deep Recurrence for Dynamical Segmentation Models
relevance_reason: U-Net with an output-to-input feedback loop (predictive-coding style) iterated with the same weights; small synthetic study.
one_sentence: Adds a predictive-coding-inspired feedback loop from output to input of a U-Net, stabilized by softmax projection and exponential decay; on a synthetic segmentation task the feedback model is more robust to noise and more data-efficient than the feedforward one.
key_contributions: Output-to-input recurrent feedback with stabilizing softmax projection and exponential decay.
Controlled noise and low-supervision experiments.

setup.loops_train: t = 5 steps (feedforward error approximation matched at t = 5)

claims.claim: The feedback model reaches above-random performance with two training examples while the feedforward model needs at least four.
claims.regime: iso_param (same U-Net with/without feedback; compute higher)
claims.evidence_quote: Notably, feedback achieves above random performance with just two training examples, while the feedforward model requires at least four.

limitations: Synthetic task only.
survey_notes: Beyond-language (vision): small-scale evidence that recurrent refinement improves data efficiency and noise robustness.

title: MazeNet: An Accurate, Fast, and Scalable Deep Learning Solution for Steiner Minimum Trees
relevance_reason: Recurrent conv blocks trained on small mazes with DT-style progressive loss, iterated more on larger instances, with a termination-condition halting module.
one_sentence: Reframes obstacle-avoiding rectilinear Steiner minimum tree as maze solving with a recurrent CNN trained on few-terminal mazes and scaled by more iterations; a termination-condition module halts once a valid path is found, giving perfect accuracy and faster runtime than exact solvers.
key_contributions: Progressive training (random n no-grad iterations, then k with-grad iterations, n+k below a maximum) following Bansal et al.
Termination Condition module checking the intermediate output to halt iteration and avoid oscillation between near-equal paths.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: mazes with a small number of terminals
setup.loops_test: more iterations for larger mazes (e.g., 30 then batches of 10)
setup.baselines: classical exact and approximate OARSMT algorithms (Kou, Mehlhorn)

claims.claim: Training on mazes with few terminals suffices; larger instances are solved by reusing the same pretrained recurrent blocks, reaching perfect accuracy and lower runtime than exact algorithms.
claims.evidence_quote: we only need to train the RCNN blocks on mazes with a small number of terminals; larger mazes can be solved by replicating the same pre-trained blocks to create a larger network.

limitations: Termination module adds overhead; outputs can oscillate between equidistant paths without it.
survey_notes: Lineage / capabilities: application of the Deep Thinking recipe (progressive loss, test-time iteration scaling) to an NP-hard routing problem, plus an explicit verification-based halting rule; illustrates that oscillation (not only divergence) is a failure mode of extended iteration.

title: Exploring Learngene via Stage-wise Weight Sharing for Initializing Variable-sized Models
relevance_reason: Trains an auxiliary model whose layers share weights within each stage, then expands the shared layers to initialize models of varying depth; sharing used for initialization, not looping at inference.
one_sentence: Stage-wise weight sharing learns compact 'learngene' layers by distillation into an auxiliary model with shared weights per stage, then expands them to initialize variable-depth ViTs, cutting training cost about 6.6x on ImageNet-1K.
key_contributions: Auxiliary model with weights shared within each stage, trained by distillation from a large model.
Expansion of stage-wise shared layers to initialize models of variable depth.

claims.claim: SWS-initialized models beat from-scratch training while reducing total training cost about 6.6x.
claims.evidence_quote: Extensive experiments on ImageNet-1K demonstrate that SWS achieves consistent better performance compared to many models trained from scratch, while reducing around 6.6x total training costs.

survey_notes: Training section (initialization / growth): tied-then-untied expansion is the reverse of retrofitting a dense model into a looped one; relevant to depth-growth curricula and to initializing untied models from looped ones.

title: Computing a human-like reaction time metric from stable recurrent vision models
relevance_reason: Uses evidence accumulation over iterations of stable (C-RBP-trained) recurrent vision models to derive a reaction-time metric.
one_sentence: Defines a subjective-logic uncertainty metric accumulated over recurrent iterations of stable recurrent vision models and shows it aligns with human reaction-time patterns across four visual decision tasks.
key_contributions: Reaction-time metric from evidence accumulation across recurrent steps.
Alignment with human RT patterns on perceptual grouping, mental simulation and scene categorization.

claims.claim: An evidence-accumulation metric over recurrent iterations matches patterns of human reaction times across four tasks.
claims.evidence_quote: We demonstrate that our metric aligns with patterns of human reaction times for stimulus manipulations across four disparate visual decision-making tasks

venue: 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023)
survey_notes: Mechanisms: number of iterations needed to accumulate evidence as an interpretable difficulty signal, analogous to halting-step analyses in adaptive looped models.

title: Iterative Forward Tuning Boosts In-Context Learning in Language Models
relevance_reason: Training-free repeated forward passes over demonstrations that accumulate information in key-value memories before answering; iteration over the context rather than layer looping.
one_sentence: Splits ICL into a Deep-Thinking stage that runs multiple forward iterations over demonstrations with an iterative enhanced attention that updates key-value memories, then a test stage that uses the refined memories; outperforms vanilla ICL across benchmarks without training.
key_contributions: Iterative enhanced attention that mixes previous-iteration KV memories with current information, without parameter updates.
Two-stage ICL (Deep-Thinking on demonstrations, then test).

claims.claim: Running multiple forward iterations over demonstrations and refining KV memories improves ICL over a single pass, without training.
claims.evidence_quote: This mechanism operates by manipulating the Key-Value matrices without training, fostering enhanced understanding capabilities in LLMs by thinking demonstrations multiple times.

survey_notes: Retrofit / training-free: a training-free 'loop' over the prompt that iteratively rewrites KV memories; conceptually close to training-free looping of pretrained LLMs but the recurrence is over passes of the context, not per-token depth.

title: Recurrent networks improve neural response prediction and provide insights into underlying cortical circuits
relevance_reason: Recurrent convolutional layers iterated on static images to predict V1/V2 neural responses; interprets recurrence as an ensemble of path lengths.
one_sentence: Adding recurrent convolutional layers to CNN models of macaque V1/V2 neurons robustly improves response prediction across thousands of hyperparameter settings; recurrence is interpreted as an ensemble of feedforward paths of different lengths.
key_contributions: Recurrent conv extension of neural-response prediction models across three datasets.
Path-ensemble view of unrolled recurrence explaining differential gains.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: three datasets of macaque V1 and V2 single-neuron responses

claims.claim: Recurrence acts as an ensemble over effective feedforward paths of varying lengths, which explains its gains.
claims.evidence_quote: We propose the recurrent circuit can be conceptualized as a form of ensemble computing, with each iteration generating more effective feedforward paths of various path lengths

survey_notes: Mechanisms: the path-ensemble interpretation of unrolled recurrence (residual paths of many lengths) is a useful lens for why looped residual models behave like ensembles of shallower networks.

title: ReSet: Learning Recurrent Dynamic Routing in ResNet-like Neural Networks
relevance_reason: Recurrently selects computational units from a learned shared set per input, so units can be reused along an input-dependent route.
one_sentence: A ResNet-like model that, at each step, dynamically selects which computational unit from a learned set to apply to each image, learning class-specific routes; beats ResNet-38 on the CIFAR-10.1 test set.
key_contributions: Recurrent dynamic routing over a learned pool of computational units.
Analysis of learned routes: similar images take similar routes.

setup.benchmarks: CIFAR-10.1 test set

claims.claim: Dynamic per-input selection of units from a shared pool beats the original ResNet-38 on CIFAR-10.1.
claims.evidence_quote: We compare our model to ResNet-38 architecture and achieve better results than the original ResNet on CIFAR-10.1 test set.

survey_notes: Design space precursor of mixture-of-recursions / routed shared blocks (input-dependent choice of which shared module to apply at each step).

title: State-Denoised Recurrent Neural Networks
relevance_reason: Inserts an attractor network iterated for multiple internal steps per sequence step to denoise RNN hidden states (depth recurrence nested in time recurrence).
one_sentence: Adds attractor dynamics trained with an auxiliary denoising loss that run several internal steps per external sequence step to clean up hidden states, improving generalization over a generic RNN and over attractor dynamics without the auxiliary loss.
key_contributions: Attractor network iterated per time step to map noisy hidden states back to previously seen states.
Auxiliary denoising loss to train the attractor.

setup.baselines: generic RNN; SDRNN without auxiliary loss

claims.claim: Multiple internal attractor steps per sequence step with a denoising loss improve generalization over a generic RNN and over the same model without the auxiliary loss.
claims.evidence_quote: On a range of tasks, we show that the SDRNN outperforms a generic RNN as well as a variant of the SDRNN with attractor dynamics on the hidden state but without the auxillary loss.

survey_notes: Lineage: early 'think several internal steps per token' design (ponder-like inner loop inside a sequence RNN), with fixed-point (attractor) state cleanup.

title: Recurrent Residual Convolutional Neural Network based on U-Net (R2U-Net) for Medical Image Segmentation
relevance_reason: Recurrent convolutional layers (same weights unfolded over a few time steps) inside U-Net blocks; recurrence used for feature accumulation at equal parameter count.
one_sentence: Replaces U-Net conv blocks with recurrent (residual) convolutional layers unfolded over a few steps, giving better medical image segmentation than U-Net and ResU-Net at the same number of parameters.
key_contributions: Recurrent residual conv units in U-Net (RU-Net, R2U-Net).
Evaluation on retina vessel, skin lesion and lung segmentation.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: retina blood vessel, skin cancer, lung lesion segmentation

claims.claim: Recurrent residual conv layers give better segmentation than U-Net at the same number of parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: it allows us to design better U-Net architecture with same number of network parameters with better performance for medical image segmentation.

survey_notes: Beyond-language (vision): small, widely cited example of iso-param recurrence gains within blocks; weak controls.

title: Implicit Feature Refinement for Instance Segmentation
relevance_reason: Replaces four stacked mask-head convolutions with one weight-shared residual block solved to a fixed point (implicit, infinite-depth refinement).
one_sentence: Finds that weight-sharing conv blocks are competitive with four consecutive convolutions in instance-segmentation heads, and builds an implicit equilibrium refinement module that improves Mask R-CNN by about 1% AP with 30% of the mask-head parameters.
key_contributions: Empirical comparison of refinement strategies: stacked vs weight-shared blocks.
Implicit feature refinement via fixed-point iteration of a single residual block; plug-and-play for image and video instance segmentation.

setup.baselines: Mask R-CNN and other instance segmentation frameworks with stacked conv heads

claims.claim: An implicit weight-tied refinement block improves Mask R-CNN mask AP by about 1% with 30% of the mask-head parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: Experiments on the COCO and YouTube-VIS benchmarks show that our IFR achieves improved performance on state-of-the-art image/video instance segmentation frameworks, while reducing the parameter burden

claims.claim: The usual four consecutive (untied) convolutions are unnecessary; weight-sharing blocks are competitive.
claims.evidence_quote: which reveals that the widely-used four consecutive convolutions are not necessary. As an alternative, weight-sharing convolution blocks provides competitive performance.

numbers.what: Mask R-CNN AP gain and mask-head parameter fraction
numbers.value: about 1% AP with 30.0% of mask-head parameters
numbers.quote: while reducing the parameter burden (e.g.1% AP improvement on Mask R-CNN with only 30.0% parameters in mask head).

survey_notes: Beyond-language (vision): component-level DEQ in a detector head, in the same family as DEQ-Decoder (journal t:deep equilibrium object detection and segmentation).

key: t:energy aware deep learning on gpus through parameter sharing and mixed precision training
title: Energy-Aware Deep Learning on GPUs through Parameter Sharing and Mixed Precision Training
relevance_reason: Systems benchmark showing ALBERT's cross-layer parameter sharing does not save time or memory relative to DistilBERT on A100s.
one_sentence: Benchmarks six models on multi-GPU A100s across FP32/TF32/BF16; despite fewer parameters, parameter-sharing ALBERT is up to 2.2x slower with up to about 3x higher GPU memory than DistilBERT, attributed to activations from deep unrolling.
key_contributions: Performance/energy trade-off analysis of parameter sharing and mixed precision.
Samples-per-Joule efficiency metric across models.

setup.model_sizes: six models incl. ALBERT, DistilBERT, TinyLlama, CNNs
setup.benchmarks: throughput, GPU memory, samples/Joule

claims.claim: Parameter sharing (ALBERT) is slower and more memory-hungry in training than a conventional smaller model, because unrolled depth creates many activations.
claims.evidence_quote: ALBERT is empirically up to 2.2× slower and triggers up to ~ 3× higher GPU memory footprint than DistilBERT

numbers.what: ALBERT vs DistilBERT slowdown and memory
numbers.quote: First, contrary to its smaller parameter count, ALBERT is empirically up to 2.2× slower and triggers up to ~ 3× higher GPU memory footprint than DistilBERT

limitations: Abstract only; ALBERT and DistilBERT differ in depth, width and training, so this is not a controlled sharing ablation.
venue: 2025 IEEE/SBC SBAC-PAD Workshops (corpus metadata)
survey_notes: Systems: confirms that weight sharing saves parameters, not activation memory or time (consistent with SC-NO 2508.20650 and FlexiGPT 2501.14713).

key: t:deep residual weight sharing attention network with low rank attention for visual question answering
title: Deep Residual Weight-Sharing Attention Network With Low-Rank Attention for Visual Question Answering
relevance_reason: Every stacked attention layer of a VQA model uses the same parameters (fully weight-tied depth) with low-rank attention units.
one_sentence: Lightweight VQA model in which every stacked residual weight-sharing attention layer uses the same parameters, with low-rank attention units; competitive on VQA-v2, GQA and CLEVR with far fewer parameters.
